facts: In Norse mythology, the god Thor did not just own a mighty hammer; he also wore a magical belt called Megingjörð that doubled his already immense divine strength when tightened.

According to ancient Greek myth, the primordial goddess Gaia gave birth to Typhon, a horrific serpentine monster so massive that his head brushed the stars and his outstretched hands spanned continents.
In Japanese folklore, the Jorōgumo is a shape-shifting spider demon that can transform into a stunningly beautiful woman playing a biwa instrument to lure unsuspecting travelers into its trap.
In Celtic mythology, the Morrígan is a fierce phantom queen associated with war and fate who frequently appears on battlefields in the shape of a screaming hooded crow.
According to Hindu mythology, the mythical mountain Meru is believed to be the sacred center of all physical, metaphysical, and spiritual universes, serving as the abode of Brahma.
In Aztec mythology, the underworld known as Mictlan is not a fiery hell, but a nine-tiered, freezing-cold subterranean labyrinth that souls must spend four years navigating before finding final rest.
In Polynesian mythology, the demigod Maui used a magical fishhook carved from his grandmother's jawbone to haul entire island chains up from the depths of the Pacific Ocean.
According to Slavic folklore, Baba Yaga is a ferocious witch who lives deep in the forest inside a bizarre hut that scuttles around on giant, clanking chicken legs.
In ancient Egyptian mythology, the demon Ammit—part crocodile, part lion, and part hippopotamus—sat beside the scales of Ma'at to devour the heavy hearts of unworthy souls.
According to Inuit mythology, the sea goddess Sedna rules the frigid ocean depths, and storms are created when shamans travel down to comb her tangled, hairless sealskin locks.
In ancient Mesopotamian myth, the goddess Ishtar descended into the seven gates of the underworld, stripping away a piece of her divine clothing and power at every single threshold.
According to Arthurian legend, the Lady of the Lake lived beneath the waters of an enchanted mere, holding the magical sword Excalibur until the right hero came to claim it.
In Yoruba mythology, Oya is the fierce goddess of the winds, lightning, and fertility, who guards the gates separating the living world from the realm of the ancestors.
According to Chinese mythology, the Moon Goddess Chang'e achieved immortality and floated up to the moon after accidentally drinking an entire vial of elixir meant for her husband.
In indigenous Australian Dreamtime mythology, the Rainbow Serpent carved out valleys, riverbeds, and mountain ranges as it slithered across the barren surface of the primordial earth.
According to Persian mythology, the Simurgh is a magnificent, wise bird so ancient that it has witnessed the destruction of the world three times over.
In Norse mythology, the trickster god Loki once gave birth to Sleipnir, an extraordinary eight-legged gray horse that could gallop across both air and land with unmatched speed.
According to Greek myth, the giant bronze automaton Talos patrolled the shores of Crete three times a day, throwing massive boulders at foreign ships to defend the island.
In Japanese folklore, Kitsune are magical fox spirits that gain multiple tails, incredible wisdom, and celestial power as they grow older and wiser over centuries.
According to Celtic tradition, the Púca is a mischievous shapeshifting creature of the night that can bring either tremendous good fortune or total chaos to rural farms.
In Hindu mythology, the celestial ocean of milk was churned using the serpent king Vasuki as a churning rope wrapped around Mount Mandara to extract the nectar of immortality.
According to Aztec lore, the fire serpent Xiuhcoatl was wielded as a devastating weapon by the sun god Huitzilopochtli to vanquish his hostile siblings at birth.
In Polynesian legend, the demigod Maui once lassoed the sun with ropes made of enchanted coconut fiber to slow down its rapid journey across the sky and lengthen the day.
According to Slavic folklore, the Domovoy is a protective house spirit that lives quietly behind the stove, keeping order and helping families who treat it with respect.
In ancient Egyptian myth, the sun god Ra battles the giant chaos serpent Apophis every single night beneath the earth to ensure the sun rises safely the next morning.
According to Inuit tradition, the Aurora Borealis is caused by the spirits of the dead playing a spirited game of football across the night sky using a walrus skull.
In Mesopotamian legend, the hero Gilgamesh embarked on a desperate quest for eternal life after the tragic death of his wild companion Enkidu broke his spirit.
According to Arthurian myth, Merlin was born from a supernatural union and possessed the rare ability to live time backward, remembering the future while experiencing the past.
In Yoruba mythology, Eshu is the divine trickster and messenger of the gods who stands at crossroads, testing human integrity and maintaining cosmic balance.
According to Chinese folklore, the Monkey King Sun Wukong was born from a magical stone boulder and successfully rebelled against the entire heavenly jade court.
In Norse mythology, the great wolf Fenrir grew so terrifyingly large and strong that the gods had to bind him with a magical ribbon forged from impossible things.
According to Greek myth, the sirens used their hauntingly sweet, irresistible singing voices to lure passing sailors into crashing their ships against jagged coastal rocks.
In Japanese folklore, the Tanuki are mischievous, shape-shifting raccoon dogs known for their love of sake, disguises, and playing harmless practical jokes.
According to Celtic mythology, the Tir na nÓg is an otherworldly paradise hidden across the western sea where no one ever grows old, falls ill, or experiences sorrow.
In Hindu lore, the god Ganesha gained his iconic elephant head after an unfortunate misunderstanding during a celestial guard duty outside his mother's bath chambers.
According to Aztec tradition, the god Quetzalcoatl descended into the dark underworld of Mictlan to gather old human bones and sprinkle them with his own blood to create humanity.
In Polynesian myth, the demigod Hina struck a deal with the moon to escape earthly burdens, settling permanently into the lunar surface with her traditional bark-cloth beater.
According to Slavic mythology, Koschei the Deathless hid his soul away inside a needle, which was hidden inside an egg, inside a duck, inside a hare, locked within a crystal chest.
In ancient Egyptian tradition, the weighing of the heart ceremony determined whether a soul could enter paradise by measuring its lightness against the feather of truth.
According to Inuit lore, the land spirits known as Inua inhabit every animal, plant, and natural feature, requiring hunters to show deep spiritual respect.
In Mesopotamian mythology, the epic of creation features the primal salt-water goddess Tiamat transforming into a monstrous dragon defeated by the storm god Marduk.
According to Arthurian tradition, the mystical island of Avalon served as the sacred sanctuary where King Arthur's wounds were tended after his final battle.
In Yoruba lore, Shango is the powerful deity of thunder, lightning, and justice, wielding a double-headed ritual axe that strikes down corrupt individuals.
According to Chinese mythology, the Jade Emperor established the 12 animals of the zodiac by hosting a grand swimming race across a swift heavenly river.
In Norse tradition, the goddess Freya owned a magnificent cloak of falcon feathers that allowed anyone who wore it to soar across the nine worlds at will.
According to Greek myth, the labyrinth of Crete was designed with such fiendish complexity that even its builder, Daedalus, barely escaped its twisting corridors.
In Japanese folklore, the Yuki-onna is a ghostly woman of the winter snowstorms who freezes wandering travelers to death with her freezing breath.
According to Celtic legend, the Salmon of Knowledge swam in the sacred Well of Segais, granting absolute wisdom to anyone who tasted its flesh.
In Hindu mythology, the celestial flying chariot known as the Pushpaka Vimana possessed the magical ability to seat any number of passengers and travel anywhere instantly.
According to Aztec myth, the universe has already been destroyed and recreated four times through cataclysmic floods, fires, and jaguar onslaughts.
In Polynesian tradition, the fierce fire goddess Pele carved out the smoking craters of the Hawaiian volcanoes during epic battles with her sister spirits.
According to Slavic folklore, the Rusalka are tragic water spirits who lure unsuspecting swimmers into deep river currents with haunting songs and silvery laughter.
In ancient Egyptian myth, the god Thoth won extra days of moonlight during a cosmic gambling match with the moon god Khonsu to help birth the children of Nut.
According to Inuit legend, the giant bear-like monster known as the Amarok stalks lone hunters across the arctic tundra under the cover of polar night.
In Mesopotamian folklore, Etana flew up into the highest heavens clinging to the back of a giant eagle after rescuing it from a deep serpent's pit.
According to Arthurian myth, the round table was crafted with a mysterious vacant seat known as the Perilous Seat, which would instantly kill anyone unworthy of sitting in it.
In Yoruba mythology, Oya commands the fierce winds of the tornado, representing sudden, transformative change that clears away stagnant old energies.
According to Chinese tradition, the loyal mythical beast known as the Qilin brings prosperity, peace, and auspicious serenity wherever its footsteps fall.
In Norse mythology, the Bifröst is a shimmering rainbow bridge connecting the realm of mortals to the golden halls of Asgard.
According to Greek legend, Pandora opened a forbidden jar out of curiosity, releasing all human miseries into the world while trapping hope safely inside.
In Japanese folklore, Kappa are reptilian water goblins that inhabit muddy riverbanks, drawing power from the pool of water cradled inside the concave tops of their skulls.
According to Celtic tradition, the banshee is a wailing female spirit whose haunting nocturnal cries foretell an imminent death within an ancestral family line.
In Hindu mythology, the celestial bird Garuda is the fierce, golden-feathered sworn enemy of serpents and the loyal mount of the preserver god Vishnu.
According to Aztec folklore, the magical warrior twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque journeyed down to the underworld to defeat the lords of death in a high-stakes ball game.
In Polynesian mythology, the island of New Zealand was formed when Maui's giant fishhook pulled up the massive landmass from the deep ocean floor.
According to Slavic folklore, the Firebird is a magnificent creature of blinding golden light whose glowing feathers can illuminate a dark forest entirely on their own.
In ancient Egyptian myth, the eye of Horus was torn apart during a fierce battle with Set, later healed and transformed into a powerful symbol of royal protection.
According to Inuit tradition, the great sea mother Sedna commands all marine mammals, withholding seals and whales from hunters if human taboos are broken.
In Mesopotamian mythology, Gilgamesh built a massive ark of reed and timber to survive a catastrophic divine flood orchestrated by angry deities.
According to Arthurian legend, the sword in the stone could only be drawn by the true rightful king of Britain, proving noble blood and pure spirit.
In Yoruba lore, Ogun is the fierce patron deity of iron, blacksmiths, technology, and warfare, honored for clearing paths through dense wilderness.
According to Chinese mythology, the heavenly river known as the Milky Way permanently separates the tragic star-crossed lovers Niulang and Zhinü.
In Norse folklore, the great world tree Yggdrasil holds the nine interconnected cosmic realms within its sprawling, deep-reaching roots and branches.
According to Greek myth, King Midas received a tragic golden touch from Dionysus, turning his beloved daughter and daily food into solid heavy gold.
In Japanese folklore, the Tengu are proud mountain goblins skilled in martial arts who punish arrogant priests and teach secret combat techniques to worthy warriors.
According to Celtic mythology, the children of Lir were transformed into swans by a jealous stepmother and forced to wander cold lakes for centuries.
In Hindu tradition, the sacred river Ganges cascaded down from the heavens with such devastating force that the god Shiva had to catch its waters in his hair.
According to Aztec lore, the rain god Tlaloc presided over an earthly paradise of eternal spring filled with lush vegetation, cascading streams, and singing birds.
In Polynesian myth, the mischievous demi-god Maui stole fire from the underworld guardian Mahuika by tricking her into giving up her burning fingernails.
According to Slavic mythology, the Morana is a goddess of winter and death whose seasonal effigy is ritually drowned in rivers every spring to welcome new life.
In ancient Egyptian tradition, the jackal-headed god Anubis guided wandering souls through the winding pathways of the desert underworld.
According to Inuit lore, the moon spirit Ajija or a wandering celestial hunter guides lost travelers safely across winter snowscapes.
In Mesopotamian myth, the goddess Inanna commanded lions and owls, embodying both fierce warfare and passionate fertility.
According to Arthurian tradition, the wizard Merlin engineered Stonehenge, magically transporting giant bluestones across the sea from Ireland.
In Yoruba mythology, Yemoja is the nurturing mother goddess of the ocean, rivers, and fertility, protecting pregnant women and nurturing maritime life.
According to Chinese folklore, the Eight Immortals crossed a roaring ocean by casting their magical talismans onto the water instead of boarding boats.
In Norse mythology, the ravens Hugin and Munin fly across the nine worlds every day to gather news and whispered secrets for the allfather Odin.
According to Greek legend, the wooden Trojan horse concealed Greek soldiers inside its hollow belly, allowing them to capture the city under cover of night.
In Japanese folklore, the Kitsune-bi or fox-fires dance across dark rural meadows, guiding or misleading travelers depending on the spirit's mood.
According to Celtic lore, the mysterious island of Hy-Brasil appears out of dense ocean fog only once every seven years to brief mortal visitors.
In Hindu mythology, the demon king Ravana possessed ten heads and twenty arms, representing mastery over the ten sacred vedic texts and martial arts.
According to Aztec mythology, the hummingbirds darting through tropical gardens are believed to be the reincarnated spirits of fallen eagle warriors.
In Polynesian tradition, the creation chant known as the Kumulipo details the genealogical evolution of life from the very first coral polyps.
According to Slavic folklore, the Leshy is a towering guardian spirit of the deep forest who can change his size from a blade of grass to a towering pine tree.
In ancient Egyptian myth, the god Osiris was resurrected by his devoted wife Isis, becoming the sovereign ruler and judge of the afterlife realm.
According to Inuit tradition, the giant sky creature known as Akna governs fertility and childbirth across frozen coastal settlements.
In Mesopotamian lore, the legendary king Etana sought the herb of birth by riding an injured eagle high up into the celestial throne rooms.
According to Arthurian myth, the holy grail possessed miraculous healing properties and provided endless feasting provisions to pure-hearted knights.
In Yoruba mythology, Orunmila is the master deity of wisdom, destiny, and divination, who witnessed the creation of the universe alongside the supreme creator.
According to Chinese mythology, the legendary flood hero Yu the Great spent thirteen years engineering massive river canals to tame raging deluge waters.
In Norse tradition, the fiery realm of Muspelheim was guarded by the giant Surt, who would one day burn the world to ashes with a glowing sword.
According to Greek myth, Arachne challenged the goddess Athena to a weaving contest and was transformed into the world's first spider out of spite.
In Japanese folklore, the Kappa love playing sumo wrestling matches and can be easily defeated if a human bows deeply, causing the water in their head-dish to spill out.
According to Celtic mythology, the ancient Tuatha Dé Danann possessed magical treasures including a sword that never missed and a cauldron of endless food.
In Hindu lore, the divine monkey commander Hanuman leaped across the vast ocean in a single bound to search for the kidnapped princess Sita.
According to Aztec tradition, the fierce sun god required daily nourishment of human blood and sacred hearts to keep the cosmos turning without plunging into darkness.
In Polynesian myth, the demigod Maui lifted the heavy sky higher up because it hung so low that people had to crawl on their hands and knees beneath it.
According to Slavic folklore, the Poludnica is a blistering midday sun spirit who punishes lazy field workers who stay out in the open during harvest time.
In ancient Egyptian tradition, the goddess Sekhmet was created from the fiery eye of Ra to punish rebellious mortals before being pacified with rivers of red beer.
According to Inuit lore, the powerful weather spirit Malina brings warmth and summer daylight after chasing her brother out across the eternal winter sky.
In Mesopotamian mythology, the wise god Enki kept the sacred divine decrees known as the ME stored safely inside his deep subterranean freshwater abyss.
According to Arthurian legend, the castle of Camelot was built with towering white stone walls and enchanted defensive wards designed by magical artisans.
In Yoruba lore, Babalu-Aye is the revered deity of healing, infectious disease, and physical recovery, often accompanied by faithful sacred dogs.
According to Chinese tradition, the dragon kings rule the four directional seas, controlling rainfall, typhoons, and oceanic tides.
In Norse mythology, the Valkyries ride across stormy battlefields to select the bravest fallen warriors and escort them to the eternal feasting halls of Valhalla.
According to Greek legend, the mythical island of Atlantis sank beneath the ocean waves in a single day and night of catastrophic earthquakes and floods.
In Japanese folklore, the Nue is a terrifying chimeric monster with the head of a monkey, the body of a tanuki, legs of a tiger, and a venomous serpent tail.
According to Celtic tradition, the ancient standing stones were believed to be petrified giants or magical portals leading directly to otherworldly realms.
In Hindu mythology, the cosmic serpent Shesha supports all the planets of the universe upon his thousands of jeweled hoods.
According to Aztec lore, the goddess Coatlicue wore a terrifying necklace of human hands and hearts, symbolizing the cyclical balance of birth and death.
In Polynesian tradition, the demigod Rata built a magnificent ocean voyaging canoe after forest spirits miraculously reassembled the trees he had felled.
According to Slavic folklore, the Zorya are three radiant sister goddesses guarding the chained apocalyptic hound that threatens to devour the cosmos.
In ancient Egyptian myth, the divine cow goddess Hathor welcomed deceased souls into the afterlife with refreshing food, music, and maternal comfort.
According to Inuit legend, the sea spirit Sedna protects all marine life, and her anger manifests as fierce Arctic blizzards that trap hunters on the ice.
In Mesopotamian folklore, the goddess Ishtar's descent caused all earthly fertility to cease until water of life was sprinkled upon her.
According to Arthurian myth, the knight Sir Galahad achieved the quest for the holy grail because of his absolute spiritual purity and unwavering virtue.
In Yoruba mythology, Oya commands the gates of the cemetery, acting as a fierce psychopomp who guides human spirits to their final resting place.
According to Chinese mythology, the legendary golden peaches of immortality bloomed in the celestial orchard of the Queen Mother of the West once every 3,000 years.
In Norse tradition, the mighty hammer Mjölnir possessed the magical ability to return directly to Thor's hand like a boomerang after being thrown.
According to Greek myth, Icarus flew too close to the sun with wax-and-feather wings built by Daedalus, plunging into the sea when the heat melted his bindings.
In Japanese folklore, the Jorōgumo transforms into a seductive weaver, trapping lonely victims in unbreakable spider silk threads.
According to Celtic mythology, the hero Cú Chulainn possessed a terrifying battle-frenzy known as the ríastrad that distorted his physical body into a monstrous shape.
In Hindu lore, the celestial weapon Brahmashira Astra was capable of destroying entire planetary systems and boiling away the oceans with intense heat.
According to Aztec tradition, the god Tezcatlipoca carried a magical obsidian mirror that could see into the secret thoughts and dark deeds of every mortal.
In Polynesian myth, the giant bird-man deity Make-make created humanity on Easter Island after speaking with a miraculous talking sea shell.
According to Slavic folklore, the Vodyanoy is a malevolent water sprite who sits on mill wheels and drags careless swimmers down to serve as his underwater slaves.
In ancient Egyptian tradition, the scarab beetle was revered as a powerful symbol of rebirth and creation, mirroring the daily journey of the sun.
According to Inuit lore, the great northern lights are the luminous playground spirits dancing across the polar winter nights.
In Mesopotamian mythology, the epic hero Gilgamesh planted a magical garden and sought the secret plant of eternal youth at the ends of the earth.
According to Arthurian legend, the sword Excalibur was accompanied by a magical scabbard that rendered its wearer completely immune to fatal blood loss.
In Yoruba lore, Ogun invented metalworking and clearing tools, serving as the foundational patron of all modern engineers, drivers, and mechanics.
According to Chinese tradition, the moon rabbit pounds medicinal elixirs of life inside a magical mortar under the shade of a cassia tree.
In Norse mythology, the trickster Loki once shaved off the golden hair of the goddess Sif just to play a malicious prank on the gods.
According to Greek legend, the multi-headed Hydra grew two new regeneration heads every time one of its necks was severed in combat.
In Japanese folklore, the Tanuki use magical leaf hats to transform into everyday objects or disguise themselves as traveling Buddhist monks.
According to Celtic tradition, the great cauldron of the Dagda possessed boundless magical power, providing an endless feast that could satisfy armies.
In Hindu mythology, the churning of the cosmic ocean produced the wish-granting cow Kamadhenu and the intoxicating divine nectar Amrita.
According to Aztec lore, the fire god Xiuhtecuhtli was honored with sacred hearth ceremonies to maintain warmth, domestic peace, and seasonal vitality.
In Polynesian tradition, the demigod Maui lifted his entire canoe into the starry night sky to form a celestial constellation known as the fishhook.
According to Slavic mythology, the Baba Yaga's fence is decorated with glowing human skulls that peer through the forest dark with fiery eye sockets.
In ancient Egyptian myth, the goddess Ma'at weighed human souls using an ostrich feather to maintain cosmic balance and universal harmony.
According to Inuit legend, the giant whale spirit Qiqirn protects coastal hunters from freezing ocean currents and malicious ice demons.
In Mesopotamian folklore, the goddess Inanna's ascent from the underworld required a substitute life to take her place in the dark realm below.
According to Arthurian myth, the legendary sword drawn from the stone was not Excalibur, but a separate testing blade of divine authority.
In Yoruba mythology, Shango's fierce wives represent the raging storms, lightning strikes, and torrential rains accompanying heavy tropical monsoons.
According to Chinese mythology, the Monkey King was imprisoned beneath a mountain of rock for five centuries before being freed by the monk Xuanzang.
In Norse tradition, the wolf Sköll chases the sun chariot across the sky while his brother Hati pursues the moon, destined to devour them at Ragnarök.
According to Greek myth, the winged horse Pegasus sprang forth from the neck of the Gorgon Medusa after Perseus defeated her.
In Japanese folklore, the Yuki-onna leaves no footprints behind in the snow because she glides silently above the frozen ground like a winter mist.
According to Celtic mythology, the salmon of wisdom gained all the knowledge of the world by eating sacred hazelnuts dropped from ancient riverside trees.
In Hindu lore, the god Vishnu assumes ten distinct cosmic incarnations—known as Avatars—to restore righteousness whenever chaos threatens the universe.
According to Aztec tradition, the feathered serpent Quetzalcoatl invented agriculture and gifted sacred maize seeds to starving humanity.
In Polynesian myth, the volcano goddess Pele journeyed across the Pacific in a sacred canoe, searching for an island home with deep fiery foundations.
According to Slavic folklore, the Domovoy must be offered a bowl of milk and bread behind the stove every night to prevent him from causing mischief.
In ancient Egyptian tradition, the divine boat of the sun stopped at twelve mystical gates corresponding to the twelve dark hours of the night.
According to Inuit lore, the northern lights are illuminated by dancing campfires where the spirits of ancestors gather to celebrate.
In Mesopotamian mythology, the epic of Gilgamesh contains one of the oldest surviving flood narratives recorded on clay cuneiform tablets.
According to Arthurian legend, the wizard Merlin possessed a magical crystal ball that allowed him to view distant lands and future events instantly.
In Yoruba lore, Eshu wears a hat split down the middle with contrasting colors, teaching villagers the importance of seeing multiple perspectives.
According to Chinese tradition, the mythical dragon brings auspicious rainfall, agricultural abundance, and imperial protection to earthly emperors.
In Norse mythology, the fortress of Valhalla featured roof shields made of polished gold and rafters constructed entirely from glittering spears.
According to Greek legend, King Midas washed his golden touch away in the Pactolus River, filling its riverbeds with shimmering gold flakes forever.
In Japanese folklore, Tengu are born from arrogant priests who fail to reach spiritual enlightenment, transforming into winged mountain guardians.
According to Celtic tradition, the magical harp of the Dagda could compel listeners to laugh, weep, or fall into an enchanted slumber at a whim.
In Hindu mythology, the mountain Kailash is the eternal cosmic home of the ascetic god Shiva and his divine family.
According to Aztec lore, the earth goddess Tlaltecuhtli was transformed into the sprawling landscape of valleys and rivers by Quetzalcoatl's divine intervention.
In Polynesian tradition, the demigod Maui used his magical jawbone fishhook to drag the sun across the sky at a slower pace.
According to Slavic mythology, the forest spirit Leshy often leads travelers in endless circular paths until they turn their clothes inside out.
In ancient Egyptian myth, the jackal god Anubis weighed hearts against feathers to determine eternal destiny in the hall of two truths.
According to Inuit tradition, the moon spirit Ajija watches over lost travelers and helps guide them back to warm winter igloos.
In Mesopotamian lore, the goddess Ishtar's descent caused all livestock breeding and crop growth to stop across the mortal lands.
According to Arthurian myth, the holy grail was guarded by the Fisher King, whose physical wounds mirrored the barren state of his kingdom.
In Yoruba mythology, Yemoja is depicted wearing seven skirts representing the seven deep layers of the ocean.
According to Chinese mythology, the celestial bridge of magpies forms once a year so the star-crossed lovers can reunite across the Milky Way.
In Norse tradition, the serpent Jörmungandr grew so massive that it encircled the entire world and bit its own tail in the deep ocean.
According to Greek myth, Pandora's box unleashed grief, disease, and hardship, leaving only fragile hope tucked away at the bottom.
In Japanese folklore, Kappa are easily tricked because their polite nature forces them to bow back when greeted, spilling the water that gives them strength.
According to Celtic mythology, the children of Lir endured 900 years of wandering as swans across frozen Irish lakes before finding peace.
In Hindu lore, the chariot of the sun god Surya is pulled by seven magnificent divine horses representing the colors of the rainbow.
According to Aztec tradition, the warrior twins defeated the lords of death through clever illusions and athletic skill in the underworld ball court.
In Polynesian myth, the fiery wrath of Pele created the rugged lava landscapes of the Hawaiian island chain.
According to Slavic folklore, the Rusalka comb their long, damp hair with golden combs; if their hair dries out completely, they lose their power and vanish.
In ancient Egyptian tradition, the scarb amulet was placed over the heart of mummies to prevent it from testifying against them during final judgment.
According to Inuit lore, the great bear spirit Amarok rewards brave hunters who track their prey with patience and respect.
In Mesopotamian mythology, the wise god Enki flooded the subterranean abyss to save humanity from divine wrath.
According to Arthurian legend, Camelot stood as a shining beacon of chivalry, justice, and round-table unity.
In Yoruba lore, Babalu-Aye commands miraculous recoveries from illness, reminding mortals of the resilience of life.
According to Chinese tradition, the Four Seas Dragon Kings control typhoons, rainstorms, and underwater palaces.
In Norse mythology, the ravens of Odin represent human thought and memory, flying out daily to observe the mortal realms.
According to Greek legend, the labyrinth held the ferocious Minotaur until the hero Theseus navigated its halls with a ball of thread.
In Japanese folklore, the Nue terrorized the imperial palace with its mournful cries until a brave archer shot it down with a sacred arrow.
According to Celtic tradition, the ancient standing stones served as gateways to the joyous realm of the Tuatha Dé Danann.
In Hindu mythology, the cosmic serpent Shesha rests upon the primordial waters, endlessly singing the praises of the creator.
According to Aztec lore, hummingbirds are brave warrior spirits transformed into iridescent jewels of the garden.
In Polynesian tradition, the Kumulipo creation chant traces the genealogical birth of the cosmos from deep darkness to vibrant life.
